title: Hashes, encodings & identifiers
description: Content and identifier hashing for services — never credentials: UTF-8 Base64 and the URL-safe Base64Url alphabet, SHA-256 as lowercase hex, idempotency keys from a canonical request string, Guid wire formats, the Luhn checksum, stable bucket hashing (why string.GetHashCode() must never be persisted: it is randomized per process) and hex round-trips. Nearest existing unit: jstrain-cs 19/01 (PBKDF2 password hashing) — nothing here hashes a password; these digests identify content and requests.

exercises.title: UTF-8 text to Base64 and back
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "We Base64 a customer name into a header and a French customer's `é` comes back broken. What went wrong?"

**Contract.** Base64 is a transform on **bytes**. `ToB64` turns the text into bytes with UTF-8, then Base64-encodes them; `FromB64` reverses both steps with the same encoding. The empty string is the empty string. Any mismatch (Latin-1 on one side, UTF-8 on the other) corrupts every non-ASCII character.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `string ToB64(string text)` → `Convert.ToBase64String(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(text))`
- `string FromB64(string b64)` → `Encoding.UTF8.GetString(Convert.FromBase64String(b64))`

**Worked example.** `"hi"` → bytes `68 69` → **`aGk=`** (two bytes need one `=` of padding).
exercises.explanation:
Base64 maps every 3 bytes to 4 characters, padding the last group with `=`.

For `ToB64("café")`:
- UTF-8 bytes: `63 61 66 C3 A9` — five bytes, because `é` (U+00E9) takes two
- bytes `63 61 66` → `Y2Fm`; `C3 A9` + padding → `w6k=`
- → **`Y2Fmw6k=`**

Under Latin-1 the same text is four bytes (`63 61 66 E9`) and a different string — always name the encoding on both sides.
hints: Base64 never sees characters, only bytes — so the question is which bytes a string turns into.
Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes / GetString around Convert.ToBase64String / FromBase64String.
Base64 is a byte transform, so pick the UTF-8 encoding explicitly on both directions — the accented character proving the point by occupying two bytes

exercises.title: Base64Url: the URL-safe alphabet
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our password-reset token is Base64 and some emails mangle it. Make it URL-safe — and show me the decoder side."

**Contract.** Standard Base64 uses `+`, `/` and `=` padding; all three are special in URLs. Base64Url (RFC 4648 §5) substitutes `-` for `+` and `_` for `/` and omits the padding.
- `ToUrlSafe`: swap the two characters, trim trailing `=`.
- `FromUrlSafe`: swap back, then append `=` until the length is a multiple of 4 (zero, one or two pads in valid input).

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `string ToUrlSafe(string b64)`
- `string FromUrlSafe(string s)` → padding count is `(4 - len % 4) % 4`

**Worked example.** `FromUrlSafe("abc")` → no swaps, length 3 → `(4 - 3) % 4 = 1` pad → **`abc=`**.
exercises.explanation:
The padding is redundant — the length already tells you how many bytes the last group held — which is why Base64Url can drop it and the reader can recompute it.

For `FromUrlSafe("ab")`:
- swaps: none
- length 2 → `(4 - 2) % 4` = **2** pads → **`ab==`**
- length 4 (`"ab-_"` → `"ab+/"`) → `(4 - 0) % 4` = 0 pads — the outer `% 4` is what stops a fifth character

Always re-pad before `Convert.FromBase64String`; it rejects unpadded input.
hints: Only three characters differ between the two alphabets, and one of them (=) is just padding the reader can recompute from the length.
Replace('+', '-').Replace('/', '_').TrimEnd('='); on the way back pad with new string('=', (4 - len % 4) % 4).
Swap plus for minus and slash for underscore and drop the padding on the way out, then swap back and append equals signs until the length is a multiple of four on the way in

exercises.title: SHA-256 as lowercase hex
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Compute a content hash for uploaded documents so we can dedupe them, and make it match what `sha256sum` prints."

**Contract.** Hash the UTF-8 bytes of the text with SHA-256 and render the 32-byte digest as 64 **lowercase** hex characters. `Convert.ToHexString` emits UPPERCASE — compare that against a canonical digest and every check fails. The digest is deterministic: the same input always gives the same output.

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function:
- `string Sha256Hex(string text)` → `Convert.ToHexString(SHA256.HashData(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(text))).ToLowerInvariant()`

**Worked example.** `Sha256Hex("abc")` → **`ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad`** (the FIPS 180-2 test vector).
exercises.explanation:
Three steps: text → bytes (UTF-8), bytes → digest (`SHA256.HashData`, the allocation-light static one-shot), digest → hex (`Convert.ToHexString`, then lowered).

For `Sha256Hex("")`:
- zero input bytes still produce a full 32-byte digest
- hex → `E3B0C442…B855` → lowered → **`e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855`**

That empty-input digest is worth recognizing on sight: seeing it in production usually means you hashed an empty body by mistake.
hints: Three conversions are chained here: text to bytes, bytes to digest, digest to text — and the last one has a casing surprise.
SHA256.HashData(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(text)), then Convert.ToHexString(...).ToLowerInvariant().
Hash the UTF-8 bytes with the static one-shot API and remember the built-in hex converter speaks uppercase, so lower the result before comparing against canonical digests

exercises.title: Idempotency key from a canonical request
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Clients retry POSTs on timeouts and we double-charge. Without asking clients to send a key, derive one from the request so a replay is detectable."

**Contract.** Build ONE canonical string — the method uppercased (HTTP methods are case-insensitive, so `get` and `GET` are the same request), then `\n`, the path, `\n`, the body — and hash it with the given `Sha256Hex`. The newline separators keep fields from bleeding into each other (`"/a" + "b"` and `"/ab" + ""` must not collide). Path and body are taken exactly as given.

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function (`Sha256Hex` is given above it):
- `string RequestKey(string method, string path, string body)`

**Worked example.** `RequestKey("get", "/orders", "")` → canonical `"GET\n/orders\n"` → **`423ce7202a5a43a2c12c56dc59c91073d2f54b4f8c3f08b22dfc05dbc0dfc636`** — identical to `RequestKey("GET", "/orders", "")`.
exercises.explanation:
Canonicalize first, hash second: every request that should be "the same" must produce byte-identical input to the hash.

For `RequestKey("get", "/orders", "")`:
- method `get` → `GET`
- canonical string `GET\n/orders\n` (empty body after the second newline)
- SHA-256 hex → **`423ce7202a5a43a2c12c56dc59c91073d2f54b4f8c3f08b22dfc05dbc0dfc636`**

Store the key with the response for a retention window; a replay with the same key returns the stored response instead of executing again.
hints: A hash only matches if the input bytes match exactly — so first decide which differences between two requests should NOT matter.
Sha256Hex(method.ToUpperInvariant() + "\n" + path + "\n" + body).
Uppercase the method, join method path and body with newline separators so fields cannot bleed into each other, and hash that one canonical string

exercises.title: Guid wire formats
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our URLs look like `/orders/3f2504e0-4f89-11d3-9a0c-0305e82c3301`. Product wants them shorter without changing the ids. What do you emit, and what do you accept?"

**Contract.** `ToId` renders the Guid in the `"N"` format: 32 lowercase hex digits, no dashes, no braces. `ParseAny` accepts both the compact `N` spelling and the dashed `D` spelling and returns the same Guid for either (old links keep working). `Guid.Empty` renders as 32 zeros.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `string ToId(Guid g)` → `g.ToString("N")`
- `Guid ParseAny(string s)` → `Guid.Parse(s)`

**Worked example.** `ToId(Guid.Parse("00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001"))` → dashes removed → **`00000000000000000000000000000001`**.
exercises.explanation:
A Guid is 16 bytes; the format string only changes how they are spelled. `"D"` (the default) adds four dashes, `"N"` omits them, `"B"`/`"P"` wrap in braces/parentheses.

For `ToId(Guid.Parse("00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001"))`:
- same 16 bytes, spelled without separators
- → **`00000000000000000000000000000001`**

Be strict in what you emit (always `N`) and liberal in what you accept (`Guid.Parse` understands every standard format), and URL changes never break old links.
hints: The value never changes — only its spelling. Guid.ToString takes a one-letter format specifier.
g.ToString("N") for 32 digits without dashes; Guid.Parse already accepts N, D, B and P formats.
The N format drops the dashes for clean urls while Parse accepts dashed and undashed spellings alike, so round-tripping through either representation lands on the same value

exercises.title: The Luhn checksum
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Before we call the payment provider, reject card numbers with a typo. Implement the Luhn check."

**Contract.** Walk the digits from the RIGHTMOST one leftward. The rightmost digit is taken as-is, the next one is doubled, the next as-is, and so on alternately. A doubled value above 9 has 9 subtracted (equivalently, its two digits summed). The number is valid when the total is a multiple of 10. Any character that is not `0`–`9` makes the input invalid (`false`, never an exception).

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function:
- `bool IsLuhnValid(string digits)`

**Worked example.** `"79927398713"` → from the right: 3, 1→2, 7, 8→16−9=7, 9, 3→6, 7, 2→4, 9, 9→18−9=9, 7 → total **70** → valid.
exercises.explanation:
Starting from the right matters: the check digit is always the last one, so "every second digit" must be counted from that end regardless of the number's length.

For `"79927398713"`:
- undoubled (positions 1, 3, 5… from the right): 3 + 7 + 9 + 7 + 9 + 7 = 42
- doubled: 1→2, 8→7, 3→6, 2→4, 9→9 → 28
- 42 + 28 = **70**, a multiple of 10 → valid

Luhn catches every single-digit typo and most adjacent swaps — cheap insurance before a network call.
hints: The check digit is the last one, so count positions from the right end — numbers have different lengths.
Loop i from Length - 1 down to 0 with an alternating flag; doubled d > 9 → d - 9; valid when sum % 10 == 0.

Walk from the rightmost digit leftward doubling every second one, fold any doubled value above nine back by subtracting nine, and accept when the total ends in zero — rejecting any character that is not a digit

exercises.title: Stable bucket hashing
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "We shard tenants with `Math.Abs(tenantId.GetHashCode()) % 16` and after a deploy everyone's data is 'missing'. Why — and write a hash that is safe to persist."

**Contract.** `string.GetHashCode()` is **randomized per process** (hash-flooding protection), so it must never be stored or compared across processes. Use a fixed polynomial hash instead: start `uint h = 0`; for each `char ch` in order, `h = h * 31 + ch`, letting the 32-bit arithmetic wrap (the wrap is part of the algorithm). The bucket is `h % buckets` computed in unsigned arithmetic — never negative, unlike `Math.Abs(int.MinValue)`. The empty key hashes to 0.

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function:
- `int Bucket(string key, int buckets)` → `(int)(h % (uint)buckets)`

**Worked example.** `Bucket("ab", 10)` → h = 97 × 31 + 98 = **3105** → 3105 % 10 = **5**.
exercises.explanation:
The polynomial `h * 31 + ch` is the classic Java-style string hash; doing it in `uint` gives a well-defined wrap and a non-negative remainder.

For `Bucket("api", 7)`:
- `a` (97): h = 97
- `p` (112): h = 97 × 31 + 112 = 3119
- `i` (105): h = 3119 × 31 + 105 = 96794
- 96794 % 7 = **5**

Any persisted mapping (shards, A/B cohorts, cache partitions) needs a hash whose definition you own — the runtime's is a per-process implementation detail.
hints: The output must be identical in every process forever, so the hash has to be an algorithm you write down, not one the runtime picks.
uint h = 0; foreach char: h = h * 31 + ch (uint arithmetic wraps); then (int)(h % (uint)buckets).

Accumulate in an unsigned integer multiplying by thirty-one and adding each character code, letting the overflow wrap, then take the remainder by the bucket count — unsigned math keeps the remainder non-negative

exercises.title: Bytes to hex and back
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Store a 16-byte nonce in a text column and read it back. Which spelling do you write, and which do you accept?"

**Contract.** Hex spells each byte as two characters `00`–`ff`. `ToHex` emits lowercase (the canonical form most tools print); `Convert.ToHexString` produces UPPERCASE, so lower it. `FromHex` parses two characters per byte and accepts either case. An empty array is the empty string.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `string ToHex(byte[] data)` → `Convert.ToHexString(data).ToLowerInvariant()`
- `byte[] FromHex(string hex)` → `Convert.FromHexString(hex)`

**Worked example.** `[0, 255, 16]` → `00`, `FF`, `10` → lowered → **`00ff10`**.
exercises.explanation:
Hex is the simplest binary-to-text encoding: one byte, two characters, no padding, no alphabet choices beyond case.

For `ToHex(new byte[] { 0, 255, 16 })`:
- 0 → `00`, 255 → `FF`, 16 → `10`
- `ToHexString` → `00FF10` → lowered → **`00ff10`**

Emit one canonical case so stored values compare as plain strings; parse leniently so hand-typed or third-party values still work.
hints: Hex is two characters per byte — the only decision left is letter case, on the way out and on the way in.
Convert.ToHexString(data).ToLowerInvariant() and Convert.FromHexString(hex) (which accepts both cases).
Hex encoding is two characters per byte with the framework emitting uppercase, so lower it for canonical output while the parser happily reads either case back into the same bytes
